items.title: Bitcoin's Rally Momentum and Near-Term Catalysts
points: Bitcoin surged above $86,000 on September 21, its highest level since January, despite Fed rate hikes and the Senate's rejection of the Clarity Act (a proposed law meant to clarify crypto regulation).
It absorbed a Fed rate hike, a Bank of Japan hike, and the Clarity Act rejection without falling below $75,000.

Over $877 million in crypto short positions (bets that prices will fall, which get forcibly closed—'liquidated'—when losses exceed margin deposits) were liquidated in 24 hours, signaling aggressive short-covering.
Three macro events over the next three weeks could determine if the rally holds: a Trump-Xi summit (September 24), the PCE price index release (September 30), and a jobs report (October 2).
Prediction markets show 74% odds Bitcoin reaches $87.5K, 44% for $90K, but only 5% for $100K, showing fading conviction at higher price targets.
Some analysts warn this could be a 'bull trap' (a false recovery followed by a sharp price decline) rather than a sustainable rally.

items.title: Institutional Accumulation Signals Continued Bullishness
points: Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy bought $76 million more BTC, bringing holdings to 845,000 BTC, near its June record after bottoming at 840,447 BTC in August.
Bitmine Immersion Technologies, backed by analyst Tom Lee, added 27,562 ETH (~$74 million) this week, continuing an unbroken buying streak and declaring a crypto bull market 'underway.'

Apple and Google are hiring senior crypto talent focused on consumer payments and institutional blockchain, hinting at stablecoin (a cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset like the US dollar) initiatives and signaling mainstream adoption momentum.

items.title: Regulatory Landscape Shift After Clarity Act Defeat
points: The Senate rejected the Clarity Act, which would have set clearer legal definitions for crypto assets, leaving regulatory control with the SEC and CFTC instead.
This creates near-term uncertainty but removes a potential legislative constraint on how these agencies regulate the industry going forward.
